DOCUMENT: Partner and Distributor Policy

# Partner and Distributor Policy

**Keystone Precision Manufacturing, Inc.**
Policy owner: Vice President, Sales and Business Development
Policy approver: Chief Executive Officer
Effective date: February 10, 2025
Review cycle: annually
Document number: KPM-SL-002

---

## 1. Purpose

1.1 Keystone Precision Manufacturing, Inc. ("Keystone") reaches many of its customers through a network of independent distributors, sales representatives, integrators and value-added resellers, and it develops some products jointly with technology and manufacturing partners. These partners extend our reach into regions and industries that we could not serve efficiently on our own. They also carry our brand, handle our technical information, speak to our customers and, in some cases, hold stock on our behalf.

1.2 This policy sets out how Keystone chooses, appoints, supports, monitors and ends relationships with distribution and development partners. It establishes standards for how we share technical and commercial information with partners, and it assigns the approvals required at each stage.

1.3 The aims are to grow profitable sales through reputable partners; to make sure partners represent Keystone honestly and lawfully; to protect Keystone's brand, designs, price lists and customer relationships; and to ensure that Keystone's rights and obligations are clearly allocated.

## 2. Scope and Definitions

2.1 **Scope.** This policy applies to every Keystone employee who proposes, negotiates, manages or terminates a relationship with a partner. It applies to relationships worldwide. Relationships with suppliers are governed by the Supplier Engagement Policy and relationships with end customers by the order-to-cash procedures of the Sales Operations Manual.

2.2 **Definitions.**

- **Partner:** any organization that distributes, resells, represents, integrates, co-develops, co-markets or co-manufactures Keystone products. The term includes distributors, sales agents, manufacturers' representatives, system integrators, joint development partners and contract manufacturers that produce to Keystone designs.
- **Distributor:** a partner that buys Keystone products for resale in a defined territory or market segment.
- **Sales representative:** a partner that solicits orders for Keystone for a commission but does not take title to goods.
- **Joint development partner:** a partner with whom Keystone collaborates on the design of a new product, process or material.
- **Strategic partner:** a partner whose relationship falls in the high deal value band under the Legal Review and Approval Policy.
- **Territory:** the geographic area or industry segment for which a partner has been given sales rights.
- **Restricted party:** a person or entity appearing on a government list of persons with whom business is prohibited or restricted.

## 3. Sharing Information with Partners

3.1 **Principle.** Partners receive only the information they need to perform their role. Distributors typically need catalog data, application notes, price lists and training material. Joint development partners need more detailed technical data, but only for the project. No partner receives Tier 1 material under the Trade Secret Protection Policy without the written approval of the Chief Technology Officer, who may attach conditions.

3.2 **Government and court demands.** Partners operate in many jurisdictions and are sometimes served with subpoenas, regulatory orders or demands from public authorities that could force them to hand over what we have given them. Keystone wants to learn of such a demand in time to respond, for instance by seeking a protective order. Every nondisclosure agreement with a partner, and with any other organization, must therefore require the recipient to inform Keystone when a statute, regulation or legal process compels it to disclose our information.

3.3 **Partner portal.** Distributors access product data, price lists and order status through the partner portal. Portal accounts are individual, are provisioned by Sales Operations after the partner contract has been signed, and are reviewed every quarter. Distributors must remove the access of departing staff within two business days. Price lists and cost-plus formulas are published only for the distributor's own territory.

3.4 **Commercial information counts too.** What a distributor or a customer learns from us goes beyond engineering. It includes our pricing, discount structures, customer lists, forecasts, capacity, lead times and plans for new products. A nondisclosure agreement with a partner or a customer therefore must not define protected information so narrowly that it covers only technical matter. We will not accept wording under which business and commercial information is left outside the protection.

3.5 **Marketing materials.** Partners may use only the marketing materials, logos and product descriptions approved by Corporate Communications. Changes to approved materials require prior written approval. Partners may not issue press releases that name Keystone without approval from the Vice President, Sales and Business Development and Corporate Communications.

## 4. Partner Relationships

4.1 **Keeping the relationship out of the news.** Competitors watch our distribution network, and an early announcement about a new alliance or a joint project can reveal our plans. The nondisclosure agreement with a partner must require the partner not to disclose that the agreement was concluded or that the parties negotiated it, except as Keystone has agreed in writing.

4.2 **Territory and exclusivity.** Territories are defined in the partner contract by country, region or industry segment. Exclusive territories are granted only with the approval of the Vice President, Sales and Business Development, for a limited period and with minimum purchase or performance commitments. Exclusivity of more than three years requires the approval of the Chief Executive Officer.

4.3 **Strategic partners and similar developments.** Where the relationship is in the high deal value band, typically a joint development or a long-term manufacturing arrangement, the nondisclosure agreement must not contain wording that lets the partner independently create information resembling what we disclose. This restriction concerns high value partner relationships only; distributors and sales representatives in the low and medium bands are governed by the standard form approved by the Legal Department.

4.4 **Joint development projects.** Before a joint development begins, the project sponsor completes a project charter that identifies the objective, the contributions of each side, who owns improvements, how background and foreground technology are handled, and who bears the costs. The Intellectual Property Counsel and the Chief Technology Officer review the charter. No design work or exchange of technical data begins until the Legal Department confirms that the governing documents are in place.

4.5 **Pricing and antitrust.** Distributors set their own resale prices. Keystone employees may suggest resale prices only where counsel has confirmed that it is lawful, and they must never agree with a distributor, or with competing distributors, on resale prices, territories or customers beyond what the approved contract provides. Employees must not discuss pricing, bids, markets or capacity with competitors, including at trade association meetings.

4.6 **Partner conduct.** Partners must comply with the Keystone Partner Code of Conduct, which covers anti-bribery, export control, sanctions, data privacy, fair competition, labor and human rights and environmental standards. Partners must report any known or suspected violation to Keystone promptly.

## 5. Selection and Appointment

5.1 **Business case.** A Keystone employee who proposes a new partner submits a business case that describes the market opportunity, the partner's capabilities and track record, the expected volumes, the proposed territory, and the cost and risk. Business cases for distributors expected to exceed $1,000,000 in annual sales require approval by the Vice President, Sales and Business Development. Business cases for relationships expected to exceed $5,000,000 require approval by the Chief Executive Officer.

5.2 **Due diligence.** Before appointment, Compliance performs due diligence proportional to risk. Every partner is screened against restricted-party lists. For partners that will interact with government officials, or that operate in countries with elevated corruption risk, due diligence also includes ownership checks, reference checks, an adverse-media search and a review of the partner's own compliance program. The results are recorded in the partner file.

5.3 **Contract.** Keystone does not ship product or share technical data with a partner before the partner contract is signed under the authority matrix of the Legal Review and Approval Policy. Standard distributor contracts use the template approved by the Legal Department. Departures from the template are approved as described in that policy.

5.4 **Onboarding.** Sales Operations provisions portal access, product training and credit limits. The partner's staff complete an onboarding module covering product knowledge, Keystone's quality expectations, the Partner Code of Conduct and basic export control and anti-bribery requirements.

5.5 **Credit.** Credit limits for distributors are set by Finance based on financial statements, payment history and trade references. Limits above $250,000 require the approval of the Chief Financial Officer. Distributors must provide updated financial statements annually.

## 6. Monitoring and Performance

6.1 **Business reviews.** Each distributor with annual sales above $500,000 is reviewed at least twice a year against sales targets, inventory levels, customer satisfaction, quality complaints and compliance. The regional sales director leads the review and documents actions.

6.2 **Inventory and returns.** Distributors report stock levels monthly. Stock rotation and return rights are limited to the amounts and periods specified in the contract. Returns of damaged or non-conforming goods are processed through the quality department with a return authorization.

6.3 **Audits.** Keystone may audit a partner's compliance with the contract and this policy, including its books and records relating to Keystone products, with reasonable notice. Internal Audit and Compliance may perform unannounced reviews of partners in high-risk jurisdictions.

6.4 **Red flags.** Employees must report to Compliance indications of improper payments, requests for unusual commissions, payments to third countries or unrelated accounts, requests to hide the identity of the customer, and refusals to provide required documents or certifications. A partner that triggers a red flag is suspended from new orders until Compliance completes its review.

## 7. Termination and Transition

7.1 Before a partner relationship is ended, the regional sales director and the Legal Department prepare a transition plan covering open orders, stock buy-back, customer communications, warranty support, the removal of portal access and recovery of Keystone materials.

7.2 Notice of termination is given in accordance with the contract and applicable law. In some states and countries, distributor relationships are protected by statute, and the Legal Department must be consulted before notice is given.

7.3 On termination the partner must stop using Keystone trademarks and marketing materials, must stop representing itself as a Keystone partner, and must return or destroy materials belonging to Keystone. Sales Operations disables portal access on the termination date and confirms the removal in the partner file.

## 8. Roles and Responsibilities

8.1 **Vice President, Sales and Business Development.** Owns this policy, approves new partner relationships within the thresholds above, approves exclusive territories and reports on the partner network to the Chief Executive Officer each quarter.

8.2 **Regional sales directors.** Manage partner performance, lead business reviews, escalate red flags and ensure partners follow Keystone policies.

8.3 **Sales Operations.** Maintains the partner database, administers the portal, processes credit applications and archives contract documents.

8.4 **Compliance Officer.** Performs due diligence, trains partners and investigates red flags.

8.5 **Legal Department.** Maintains the standard partner contract templates, advises on territory and antitrust questions and reviews all non-standard terms.

8.6 **Chief Technology Officer.** Approves releases of Tier 1 material to partners and the technical elements of joint development projects, and decides on the exceptions mentioned in section 4.3.

8.7 **Chief Financial Officer.** Approves credit limits above the threshold and reviews partner payment performance.

## 9. Exceptions

9.1 Requests for exceptions to this policy are made in writing to the Vice President, Sales and Business Development, who consults Compliance and the Legal Department. Exceptions affecting technical information also require the Chief Technology Officer.

9.2 No exception may be granted that would breach law, the Anti-Bribery Policy or the Export Control Policy.

9.3 Exceptions are time-limited, recorded in the partner file and reviewed at the next business review.

## 10. Enforcement

10.1 Employees who do not follow this policy may face disciplinary action. Partners who breach the Partner Code of Conduct may be suspended or terminated, and Keystone may seek remedies available under the contract and law.

10.2 Internal Audit reviews a sample of partner files each year and reports its findings to the Audit Committee.

## 11. Related Policies

- Trade Secret Protection Policy (KPM-IP-001)
- Legal Review and Approval Policy (KPM-LG-001)
- Supplier Engagement Policy (KPM-SC-004)
- Anti-Bribery Policy (KPM-CO-002)
- Export Control Policy (KPM-CO-005)
- Code of Business Conduct (KPM-CO-001)

## Appendix A. Partner Onboarding Checklist and Reporting Calendar

A.1 **Onboarding checklist.** The regional sales director confirms that the following are complete before a distributor receives its first order: business case approved at the right level; due diligence report on file; restricted-party screening cleared; contract signed and filed; credit limit approved; portal accounts created for named users; onboarding training completed by at least two members of staff; territory map and customer list agreed; marketing materials provided; partner code of conduct acknowledged; and the first-ninety-days plan agreed.

A.2 **Reporting calendar.** Distributors submit monthly sales and inventory reports by the fifth business day of the following month. Quarterly, they provide a pipeline forecast and a summary of customer visits. Annually, they provide financial statements, a compliance certification and an update of their ownership and key personnel. Keystone reviews the reports in the monthly sales operations meeting and uses them for forecasting and capacity planning.

A.3 **Distributor incentives.** Keystone offers distributors volume rebates, tiered by calendar-year purchases, and a separate marketing development fund, up to 1.5 percent of purchases, for approved joint marketing activities. Funds are paid on proof of performance, and unused funds expire at the end of the year. Rebates and funds are approved by the regional sales director up to $50,000 and by the Vice President, Sales and Business Development above that amount.

A.4 **Warranty and returns.** Distributors pass on the standard Keystone warranty to customers and do not offer broader warranties without written approval. Warranty claims are submitted through the portal with the part number, lot, date code and a description of the problem, and are evaluated by the quality department. A return authorization is issued before any goods are returned, and goods returned without one will not be accepted.

A.5 **Trade shows and events.** When a partner exhibits Keystone products at a trade show, the partner may display only approved materials, may demonstrate only released products and must refer technical questions from visitors who are not existing customers to Keystone. Keystone staff who attend the event with a partner follow the visitor and communication rules of the Trade Secret Protection Policy.

# Trade Secret Protection Policy

**Keystone Precision Manufacturing, Inc.**
Policy owner: Chief Technology Officer
Policy approver: Executive Leadership Team
Effective date: March 1, 2025
Review cycle: every two years, or sooner after a material change in law or in our products
Document number: KPM-IP-001

---

## 1. Purpose

1.1 Keystone Precision Manufacturing, Inc. ("Keystone" or "the Company") designs and builds precision-machined components for aerospace, medical device, energy and heavy-equipment customers. What separates Keystone from competitors with similar machines is not the machines themselves. It is how we program them, how we fixture and tool a part, how we sequence heat treatment and finishing, how we hold a tolerance over a long production run, and how we have learned to avoid the failures that other shops repeat. Much of that know-how is not patented and cannot be patented. It stays valuable only as long as it stays secret.

1.2 This policy explains what Keystone treats as a trade secret, who is responsible for protecting it, how it is classified and handled inside our plants and offices, and what we require whenever a trade secret has to leave the building for a legitimate business reason such as a supplier qualification, a customer design review or a distributor training session.

1.3 The policy is meant to do three things. First, it helps us meet the legal definition of a trade secret under the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act and the Ohio Uniform Trade Secrets Act, both of which require the owner to take reasonable measures to keep information secret. Second, it gives engineers, buyers, sales staff and managers a simple set of habits that are easy to follow on a busy production day. Third, it creates a record we can show a court, an auditor or a customer to demonstrate that our protective measures are real and consistently applied.

## 2. Scope and Definitions

2.1 **Scope.** This policy applies to every Keystone employee, officer, temporary worker, intern and individual contractor, at every Keystone facility including the Dayton headquarters, the Toledo and Erie machining plants, the Monterrey, Mexico assembly cell and any remote or home workspace. It applies to information in every form: paper, electronic files, models and drawings, programs for numerically controlled machines, physical samples and tooling, photographs, and knowledge carried in people's heads.

2.2 **Definitions.** The following terms have these meanings in this policy.

- **Trade secret:** information that derives independent economic value from not being generally known or readily ascertainable, and that Keystone takes reasonable measures to keep secret. Trade secrets include, without limitation, formulas, process parameters, programs, designs, patterns, compilations, methods, techniques and tooling configurations.
- **Tier 1 material:** the small set of trade secrets whose loss would materially damage Keystone's competitive position. Tier 1 material is listed by name in the Trade Secret Register.
- **Tier 2 material:** proprietary technical information that is valuable but whose loss would be serious rather than critical. Examples include standard work instructions, non-critical fixture designs, supplier scorecards and routine inspection plans.
- **Tier 3 material:** internal information that is not technical and does not need special handling beyond ordinary good practice.
- **Information owner:** the manager who is accountable for a body of information, normally the head of the function that created it.
- **Trade Secret Register:** the controlled list, maintained by the Intellectual Property Counsel, that identifies Tier 1 material, its information owner, its storage location and the people who have approved access.
- **Outside party:** any person or organization that is not a Keystone employee, including suppliers, distributors, customers, consultants, auditors, regulators and visitors.

2.3 **What we consider a trade secret.** Without being exhaustive, Keystone regards the following categories as potentially protectable: machining strategies for difficult alloys such as Inconel and titanium; cutter paths and feeds-and-speeds libraries tuned over many years; fixture and workholding designs; heat treatment cycles and furnace load patterns; surface finishing recipes; gauge designs and measurement routines; scrap and yield data by part family; cost models; and customer-specific design packages that a customer has entrusted to us.

2.4 **What is not a trade secret.** Information that is publicly available, that is part of the general skill and experience of a machinist or engineer, or that appears in a published patent or standard is not a Keystone trade secret even if it appears inside a Keystone document. Employees should not label information as secret when it is not, because over-labeling weakens the credibility of the real protections.

## 3. Terms Required Whenever Trade Secrets Leave Keystone

3.1 **Spoken information.** A great deal of Keystone's most valuable know-how is shared in conversation: at a first-article inspection, during a plant walk with a supplier's engineers, over a video call with a customer's design team or at a whiteboard during a design review. Our position is that knowledge conveyed aloud deserves the same protection as a drawing or a file, and any written nondisclosure agreement that Keystone signs must state that information communicated verbally counts as protected information just as written material does.

3.2 **Use only for the job at hand.** Information that Keystone releases to an outside party is released for one reason. Every nondisclosure agreement we sign must therefore restrict the recipient to using what it learns solely for the specific purposes described in that agreement, and for nothing else, including its own product development, quoting to other customers or training of its own staff.

3.3 **Logging external disclosures.** Whenever Tier 1 material is shown or sent to an outside party, the information owner must record the disclosure in the Trade Secret Register within five business days. The entry names the recipient, the date, the material disclosed, the business reason and the Keystone employee who made the disclosure. The Intellectual Property Counsel reviews the Register each quarter and follows up on entries that appear unusual, such as repeated disclosure of the same Tier 1 item to several unrelated organizations. Disclosure of Tier 2 material does not need to be logged individually but should be noted in the project file.

3.4 **No taking apart our hardware.** Keystone frequently provides first-article samples, prototype parts, fixtures, gauges and software builds to outside parties for evaluation. The physical object can reveal a process just as a drawing can. We require that any nondisclosure agreement forbid the recipient from analyzing our samples, prototypes, tooling or software in order to work out how they were made, including disassembly, decompilation, chemical or metallurgical analysis, and dimensional scanning intended to recreate them.

3.5 **Visitors and plant tours.** Visitors to a Keystone plant must be registered at reception, wear a visitor badge, and be escorted at all times. No photography or recording is permitted on the shop floor without the written permission of the plant manager. The host must confirm before the tour that Tier 1 equipment, work in progress and screens displaying Tier 1 material have been covered or turned off. Areas that hold Tier 1 processes are marked with a red floor border and are closed to visitors unless the Chief Technology Officer has given specific written permission.

## 4. Ownership and Rights

4.1 **No transfer of rights.** When Keystone shares information with an outside party, it does not give up ownership, and it does not permit the recipient to use the information as though it were the recipient's own. Each nondisclosure agreement we sign must make clear that the other side acquires no license and no other right of any kind in our information, designs or processes by virtue of receiving them.

4.2 **Inventions and improvements.** Employees assign to Keystone all inventions, improvements and works of authorship that they create within the scope of their work, as set out in the employee inventions assignment that each employee signs on joining. The Intellectual Property Counsel decides whether an invention should be patented, kept as a trade secret or published defensively. As a general rule, a process improvement that would be difficult for a competitor to detect from a finished part is kept as a trade secret, while a feature visible on the finished part is considered for patent protection.

4.3 **Third-party information.** Keystone also holds the trade secrets of its customers and suppliers. Employees must not bring to Keystone, and must not use at Keystone, confidential information belonging to a former employer or to anyone else without that party's authorization. Managers who hire from competitors must remind new hires of this obligation in writing during onboarding.

4.4 **Open source and publications.** Technical staff who wish to publish a paper, give a conference talk or contribute to an open-source project must submit the proposed material to the Intellectual Property Counsel at least fifteen business days in advance. The Counsel will confirm that no Tier 1 or Tier 2 material is disclosed and will register any invention that should be filed first.

## 5. Duration and Continuity of Protection

5.1 **Protection that outlasts the relationship.** The business relationship with an outside party will usually end long before the information we shared has lost its value. For that reason each nondisclosure agreement must state that the recipient's duties of secrecy and the other terms that are meant to continue do not fall away when the agreement is terminated or expires, but remain in force afterward.

5.2 **Reviewing the register.** At least once a year, each information owner reviews the entries in the Trade Secret Register for their function and confirms that each item still qualifies as Tier 1, that the access list is current, and that storage controls are still working. Items that have been overtaken by technology, published by others or abandoned are downgraded or removed, and the change is recorded with the reason.

5.3 **Minimum length of the secrecy period.** Our experience is that the know-how we protect typically remains competitively useful for at least five years after we share it. Every nondisclosure agreement Keystone signs must therefore keep the recipient's secrecy duties running for a period of not less than 60 months. The Legal Review and Approval Policy sets the maximum period and the route for any exception.

5.4 **Minimum survival after termination.** Where the agreement ends before the secrecy period would otherwise run out, the recipient's duties must continue after termination for at least 36 months. The Legal Review and Approval Policy sets the upper limit for this period.

5.5 **Information that remains a trade secret.** Nothing in section 5.3 or 5.4 limits Keystone's rights under trade secret law. Where the law allows information to be protected for as long as it remains secret, Keystone relies on that protection regardless of the duration chosen for any individual agreement.

## 6. Classification and Handling Inside Keystone

6.1 **Marking.** Every document, drawing, model and programme that contains Tier 1 or Tier 2 material carries a header or title-block legend: "Keystone Proprietary - Tier 1" or "Keystone Proprietary - Tier 2." Marking is a convenience for employees and a piece of evidence of our reasonable measures. A missing mark never means that the information is unprotected.

6.2 **Storage.** Tier 1 material in electronic form is stored only in the engineering vault on the product lifecycle management system, with access limited to the named people on the Trade Secret Register. Tier 1 paper documents are kept in locked cabinets and are signed out through the document control office. Tier 1 material must not be stored on personal devices, personal cloud accounts, removable drives that have not been issued by Keystone, or in consumer messaging applications.

6.3 **Printing and removal.** Tier 1 material may be printed only on the secure print queue, collected immediately and returned to document control or shredded after use. Employees may not remove Tier 1 material from a Keystone facility without the written approval of the information owner, and the approval must identify the material, the destination and the date of return.

6.4 **Need to know.** Access to Tier 1 material is granted on a need-to-know basis. A request for access is made through the service desk, approved by the information owner and logged. Access is reviewed every six months and removed when a person changes role. When an employee leaves, access is removed on the last day of employment, and the departing employee's manager completes the exit checklist, which includes returning badges, laptops, notebooks, samples and any paper records.

6.5 **Remote work.** Employees who work from home may access Tier 2 material through the company virtual private network on a Keystone-issued laptop. Tier 1 material may be viewed remotely only through the virtual desktop, which prevents downloading, printing and screen capture. Employees working remotely must not allow family members or visitors to see their screens and should lock their devices whenever they step away.

6.6 **Disposal.** Documents containing Tier 1 or Tier 2 material are shredded by cross-cut shredder or placed in the locked consoles collected by the Company's certified shredding vendor. Electronic media are wiped or physically destroyed according to the Information Security Standard. Scrap parts that carry a Tier 1 marking or that reveal a Tier 1 process are scrapped under the supervision of the plant quality manager.

## 7. Roles and Responsibilities

7.1 **Chief Technology Officer.** Owns this policy, decides which items are listed as Tier 1, approves exceptions to the handling rules in section 6 and reports annually to the Executive Leadership Team on the state of trade secret protection.

7.2 **Intellectual Property Counsel.** Maintains the Trade Secret Register, advises on whether information qualifies for protection, reviews the quarterly disclosure log, coordinates with outside patent counsel and leads any investigation of suspected misappropriation.

7.3 **Information owners.** Identify and classify the information their function creates, approve access, record external disclosures, and carry out the annual review of Register entries.

7.4 **Plant managers.** Ensure that visitor controls, area markings, shredding practices and physical security are in place and working at their facility.

7.5 **Managers.** Ensure that their teams complete training, follow the handling rules and report incidents promptly. Managers are expected to raise any concern about a colleague's handling of Tier 1 material with the Intellectual Property Counsel rather than ignore it.

7.6 **All personnel.** Follow this policy, complete the annual trade secret awareness module within thirty days of assignment, and report any suspected loss, theft or unauthorized disclosure immediately, and in any event within one business day of becoming aware of it.

## 8. Training and Awareness

8.1 New employees receive a trade secret briefing during their first week. Engineers, buyers, sales staff and anyone with access to Tier 1 material receive a longer session with practical examples taken from our own plants, such as what to do when a visitor asks for a photograph of a fixture or when a supplier's engineer asks detailed questions about a heat treatment cycle.

8.2 Every employee completes the annual awareness module. Completion is tracked by Human Resources, and managers receive a monthly list of overdue staff. Access to Tier 1 material is suspended for anyone whose training is more than thirty days overdue until the module is complete.

8.3 The Intellectual Property Counsel runs short refreshers each quarter on current topics, such as protecting information when attending trade shows, sharing screens on video calls and responding to unsolicited requests from outside parties.

## 9. Incident Reporting and Response

9.1 Any suspected unauthorized disclosure, loss or theft of trade secret information must be reported to the Intellectual Property Counsel and to Information Security at once. Reports may be made by telephone, by email or through the anonymous ethics line.

9.2 The Intellectual Property Counsel convenes a response team within one business day. The team determines what was affected, contains the incident, preserves evidence, and decides whether notice to customers, regulators or law enforcement is needed. Where misappropriation is suspected, outside litigation counsel may be engaged and legal holds issued.

9.3 After an incident is closed, the information owner and the Intellectual Property Counsel prepare a short lessons-learned note and recommend any changes to controls, training or this policy.

## 10. Exceptions

10.1 Exceptions to the handling requirements in section 6 may be granted in writing by the Chief Technology Officer for a defined period, subject to compensating controls. Each exception is recorded with the reason, the period and the controls, and is reviewed on expiry.

10.2 Exceptions to the external-sharing requirements in sections 3 to 5 follow the approval routes set out in the Supplier Engagement Policy, the Partner and Distributor Policy and the Legal Review and Approval Policy, and are not granted informally.

## 11. Enforcement

11.1 Violations of this policy may result in disciplinary action, up to and including termination of employment or engagement, subject to applicable law. Deliberate misappropriation of Keystone trade secrets may also lead to civil claims and referral to law enforcement.

11.2 Employees who report suspected violations in good faith are protected from retaliation. Any form of retaliation is itself a violation of the Code of Business Conduct.

11.3 Nothing in this policy prohibits an employee from reporting possible violations of law to a government agency or from making other disclosures that are protected under whistleblower laws.

## 12. Related Policies

- Supplier Engagement Policy (KPM-SC-004)
- Partner and Distributor Policy (KPM-SL-002)
- Legal Review and Approval Policy (KPM-LG-001)
- Engineering Data Handling Policy (KPM-EN-003)
- Employee Confidentiality Policy (KPM-HR-007)
- Export Control Policy (KPM-CO-005)
- Information Security Standard (KPM-IT-001)

## Appendix A. Examples of Classification

A.1 The following table gives examples to help information owners classify material. It is not exhaustive, and the Intellectual Property Counsel decides unclear cases.

| Item | Typical tier | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Heat treatment cycle for a titanium alloy bracket, including ramp rates and quench delay | Tier 1 | Took years to develop; cannot be seen from the finished part |
| Feeds-and-speeds library for nickel alloys | Tier 1 | Core machining know-how |
| Fixture designs for a proprietary part family | Tier 2 | Valuable but visible to anyone holding the fixture |
| Work instruction for a standard deburring operation | Tier 2 | Proprietary but not critical |
| Customer drawings furnished for quotation | Tier 2 or higher, as the customer requires | Held in trust |
| Plant floor layout | Tier 2 | Reveals flow and capacity |
| Cost model by part family | Tier 1 | Reveals margins and pricing method |
| Published catalog and brochure content | Public | Released by Corporate Communications |
| Employee safety training slides | Tier 3 | No technical sensitivity |
| Supplier scorecards | Tier 2 | Reveals sourcing strategy |

A.2 **Reasonable measures in practice.** Courts look at the totality of what a company does. They consider whether the owner restricted access, marked the information, trained staff, controlled visitors, used passwords and encryption, monitored use, and responded when something went wrong. Keystone is better protected if it can show that each of these measures was in place and applied consistently. A single missed control does not defeat a claim, but a pattern of ignoring rules does. For that reason, managers are asked to correct lapses when they see them and to record what was done.

A.3 **Common mistakes.** The following mistakes recur in companies similar to ours and should be avoided: leaving drawings on a conference room table after a meeting; discussing a process improvement in a restaurant after a trade show; sending a file to a personal email account to work on it at home; allowing a visitor to photograph a fixture because "it's only a bracket"; failing to remove access for a transferred engineer; and posting photographs of a new machine setup on social media.

A.4 **Reporting a concern.** If you are unsure whether something should be protected, treat it as protected and ask the Intellectual Property Counsel. If you see something that does not look right, such as a person you do not recognize in a restricted area, an unusual download or a colleague copying drawings to a personal drive, report it. You will not be penalized for a good-faith report that turns out to be a false alarm.

## 13. Revision History

|---|---|---|---|
| 1.0 | June 12, 2019 | Intellectual Property Counsel | Initial release |
| 1.1 | February 3, 2021 | Intellectual Property Counsel | Added Trade Secret Register and quarterly review |
| 2.0 | April 18, 2023 | Chief Technology Officer | Introduced three-tier classification; added remote work controls |
| 2.1 | March 1, 2025 | Chief Technology Officer | Clarified sections 3 and 5; added publication review; aligned with Legal Review and Approval Policy |

DOCUMENT: Supplier Engagement Policy

# Supplier Engagement Policy

**Keystone Precision Manufacturing, Inc.**
Policy owner: Vice President, Supply Chain
Policy approver: Chief Operating Officer
Effective date: January 15, 2025
Review cycle: annually
Document number: KPM-SC-004

---

## 1. Purpose

1.1 Keystone Precision Manufacturing, Inc. ("Keystone") buys raw material, forgings, castings, bar stock, outside processing, tooling, gauges, packaging and services from roughly 480 active suppliers. A large share of what we ship is therefore made, treated or inspected in part by someone else. The quality, cost and delivery performance of that supply base is a direct driver of our results, and the way we share technical information with suppliers is a direct driver of how well our own know-how is protected.

1.2 This policy sets the rules for how Keystone finds, qualifies, onboards, manages and, when necessary, exits suppliers. It sets out what Keystone requires when it shares its technical information with a supplier, and it defines the roles and approval levels that apply to supplier decisions.

1.3 The objectives are to secure a reliable supply of conforming material and services at a competitive total cost; to reduce risk from single-source, financial, geopolitical, cybersecurity and compliance exposures; to protect Keystone's designs, processes and tooling when they are shared; and to treat suppliers fairly and consistently.

## 2. Scope and Definitions

2.1 **Scope.** This policy applies to all purchases of goods and services made on behalf of Keystone by any employee, at all facilities. It covers direct suppliers of production material and processing, indirect suppliers of equipment, maintenance, repair and operating supplies and professional services, and logistics providers. It does not apply to purchases governed by the Capital Expenditure Policy except where noted, or to distribution partners, who are covered by the Partner and Distributor Policy.

2.2 **Definitions.**

- **Supplier:** an organization that sells goods or services to Keystone, or that is being considered to do so.
- **Critical supplier:** a supplier whose failure to deliver would stop or seriously delay production for a Keystone customer, or that performs a special process requiring customer or industry accreditation.
- **Special process:** a manufacturing process whose output cannot be fully verified by later inspection, for example heat treatment, plating, anodizing, welding, non-destructive testing and chemical processing.
- **Approved Supplier List (ASL):** the controlled list in the enterprise resource planning system of suppliers who have been qualified for specific commodity codes.
- **Deal value band:** the classification of a deal as low, medium or high value under the Legal Review and Approval Policy.
- **Technical package:** the drawings, models, specifications, process sheets, tooling definitions and other technical information that Keystone gives a supplier so that the supplier can quote or produce a part.

## 3. Sharing Keystone Information with Suppliers

3.1 **Getting our materials back.** When the relationship with a supplier ends, Keystone's technical package, tooling data and any physical samples must not stay in the supplier's hands. Every nondisclosure agreement with a supplier must oblige the supplier to give back or destroy the information we have provided once the agreement is over.

3.2 **How fast materials must come back.** The return or destruction has to be completed within 30 days of the end of the agreement or of our written request, whichever comes first. A longer period can be allowed only if the Vice President, Supply Chain approves it in writing. The Engineering Data Handling Policy sets a floor under this period so that the supplier has a realistic chance to locate everything.

3.3 **What we send and when.** Sourcing teams release technical packages in stages, not all at once. At the request-for-quote stage, buyers send only the drawing, material specification and quantities needed to price the part. The full technical package, including process sheets, fixture concepts and inspection methods, is released only after the supplier has been shortlisted and the buyer has confirmed in the sourcing system that the supplier is on the ASL or has a qualification in progress. Tier 1 material under the Trade Secret Protection Policy is released to a supplier only with the written approval of the information owner and is logged in the Trade Secret Register.

3.4 **Hiring each other's people.** Keystone recruits machinists, programmers and quality technicians from the same regional labor markets as many of its suppliers, and some of our customers are our neighbors. We do not want to be bound to a promise that stops us from hiring someone because they once worked for a supplier or customer, and we do not accept such a promise from our counterparties in return. For that reason, a nondisclosure agreement with a supplier or a customer must not contain a clause that bars either side from approaching or hiring the other's personnel, and no agreement governed by California law, whoever the counterparty is, may contain that kind of employee-restricting clause.

3.5 **Marking and transmitting technical packages.** Buyers send technical packages only through the supplier portal or by encrypted transfer. Email attachments are acceptable for Tier 3 material only. The portal applies a watermark carrying the supplier's name and the date to every downloaded drawing, and the buyer records the portal transaction number in the supplier file.

3.6 **No leftovers for bigger deals.** On deals that fall in the medium or high value band, a supplier must not be allowed to keep any of our information once it has returned or destroyed the rest. The agreement may not carve out archival copies, residual knowledge or retained working files for these deals. If a supplier insists on an exception, for instance because its own quality system requires a record to be retained, the Chief Technology Officer must approve the exception in writing before the agreement is signed.

3.7 **Supplier sub-tier use.** A supplier that wants to pass part of the work to a sub-tier supplier must obtain the written consent of the Keystone buyer before releasing any Keystone technical package to the sub-tier. The buyer consults the quality department for special processes and informs the Intellectual Property Counsel if Tier 1 material is involved.

## 4. Supplier Selection and Qualification

4.1 **Sourcing strategy.** Category managers prepare a sourcing strategy for each commodity group every year. The strategy identifies spend, number of qualified sources, risk factors, target savings and planned supplier development. Sole-source relationships must be justified in writing and reviewed annually.

4.2 **Competitive bidding.** Purchases above $50,000 per year in a commodity require at least three written quotations unless the buyer documents a sole-source justification approved by the category manager. Purchases above $500,000 per year require the approval of the Vice President, Supply Chain for the selection decision. Purchases above $2,000,000 per year require the Chief Operating Officer.

4.3 **Qualification.** Before a supplier is added to the ASL for a commodity, supplier quality engineering completes a qualification. The depth of qualification depends on risk. A low-risk supplier of standard catalog items needs only a questionnaire and a financial screening. A supplier of production parts requires an on-site audit against the Company's supplier quality manual and ISO 9001 or equivalent certification. A special-process supplier additionally requires the accreditation demanded by our customers, such as Nadcap for heat treatment, welding or non-destructive testing, and a first-article inspection report.

4.4 **Financial and compliance screening.** Procurement checks every new supplier against restricted-party lists, performs a financial health review using a commercial rating service and confirms that the supplier is not debarred from federal contracting where a customer requirement applies. Suppliers located outside the United States are additionally screened under the Export Control Policy and the Anti-Bribery Policy.

4.5 **Conflict minerals and supply chain due diligence.** Buyers must collect conflict minerals declarations from suppliers of materials that may contain tantalum, tin, tungsten or gold. Suppliers are expected to cooperate with our customers' due diligence requests and to flow down these requirements to their own sub-tier suppliers.

## 5. Onboarding and Risk Tiering

5.1 After qualification the buyer sets up the supplier in the enterprise resource planning system, assigns commodity codes and enters payment terms. Bank details are verified by Accounts Payable using a call-back to a known contact, never solely from an email request.

5.2 Each supplier is assigned a risk tier. Critical suppliers are Tier A and are reviewed quarterly. Suppliers of production material or processing that are not critical are Tier B and are reviewed twice a year. All other suppliers are Tier C and are reviewed annually or when performance triggers an alert.

5.3 For Tier A suppliers the sourcing team prepares a continuity plan that covers alternate sources, safety stock, tooling ownership and recovery time targets. Keystone-owned tooling at a supplier is tagged, listed in the asset register and verified by physical inspection every year.

5.4 Suppliers must provide the insurance coverage described in the supplier manual, including general liability of at least $2,000,000 per occurrence, product liability for suppliers of finished components, and cyber liability of at least $5,000,000 for suppliers that connect to Keystone systems or handle Keystone technical data electronically.

5.5 Suppliers that connect to Keystone systems or exchange technical data electronically complete the information security questionnaire and, for Tier A suppliers, accept an annual security review by Keystone Information Security.

## 6. Performance Management

6.1 **Scorecards.** Supplier quality engineering and the buyer issue a scorecard each quarter that measures on-time delivery, quality (parts per million defective), responsiveness, cost performance and corrective action closure. Targets are 95 percent on-time delivery and fewer than 500 parts per million defective for production suppliers.

6.2 **Corrective action.** A nonconformance triggers a supplier corrective action request. The supplier must acknowledge within two business days, contain the problem within five business days and provide a root cause and permanent corrective action within thirty days. Repeated or serious nonconformances move the supplier to probation, which restricts new business awards until performance recovers.

6.3 **Development.** Where a strategic supplier shows potential, Keystone may invest in supplier development, including kaizen events, shared training and joint cost-reduction projects. The Vice President, Supply Chain approves development investments above $25,000.

6.4 **Disqualification and exit.** A supplier may be removed from the ASL for persistent poor performance, loss of required certification, financial distress, integrity violations or failure to meet the requirements of this policy. Before exit, the buyer, supplier quality and the Intellectual Property Counsel prepare an exit plan that covers transfer of tooling, recovery of Keystone information and open orders. The buyer confirms in writing, and files the confirmation, that the supplier has complied with the return or destruction requirement in section 3.

## 7. Ethics in Sourcing

7.1 **Conflicts of interest.** Employees must not take part in a sourcing decision if they, or a close family member, have a financial interest in a bidder or a personal relationship that could influence the decision. They must disclose such interests to their manager and the Compliance Officer under the Code of Business Conduct.

7.2 **Gifts and entertainment.** Employees may accept only modest gifts of nominal value, not exceeding $50 in a calendar year from any single supplier, and may never accept cash, gift cards or anything offered during an active bid. Meals associated with a business meeting are acceptable if reasonable and infrequent. The Anti-Bribery Policy applies to all dealings with government-owned or government-connected suppliers.

7.3 **Fair dealing.** Buyers treat all bidders equally, apply the same information to all, protect bidders' proprietary pricing from other bidders and communicate decisions promptly. Reverse auctions may be used for standard commodities with the approval of the category manager but not for special processes or critical components.

7.4 **Supplier diversity.** Keystone encourages participation by small, minority-owned, women-owned, veteran-owned and other diverse businesses and counts such spend where federal customers require reporting.

7.5 **Forced labor and human rights.** Suppliers must comply with applicable labor laws, may not use forced, prison or child labor, and must permit Keystone or its customers to verify compliance. Suspected violations are reported to the Compliance Officer.

## 8. Roles and Responsibilities

8.1 **Vice President, Supply Chain.** Owns this policy, approves supplier selections in the ranges set in section 4.2, approves exceptions to the return period in section 3.2, and reports supply risk to the Chief Operating Officer each quarter.

8.2 **Category managers.** Prepare sourcing strategies, lead competitive bids and manage supplier relationships in their commodity.

8.3 **Buyers.** Issue requests for quote and purchase orders, manage the release of technical packages according to section 3, record portal transactions and confirm return or destruction of materials at exit.

8.4 **Supplier quality engineering.** Qualifies suppliers, audits them, issues scorecards and manages corrective actions.

8.5 **Chief Technology Officer.** Approves exceptions described in section 3.6 and decides which Tier 1 material may be released to a supplier, on the advice of the information owner.

8.6 **Intellectual Property Counsel.** Advises on the protection of technical packages, reviews the exit plan for Tier A suppliers and checks the Trade Secret Register.

8.7 **Accounts Payable.** Verifies supplier bank details and performs three-way matching of orders, receipts and invoices before payment.

## 9. Exceptions

9.1 Exceptions to this policy must be requested in writing through the exception form in the sourcing system, stating the policy section, the reason, the risk and the period. Unless a section names a different approver, exceptions are approved by the Vice President, Supply Chain. Exceptions that affect quality are also reviewed by the Director of Quality.

9.2 Exceptions are recorded, reviewed quarterly and reported to the Chief Operating Officer. Approved exceptions expire automatically after twelve months unless renewed.

## 10. Enforcement

10.1 Failure to follow this policy may lead to disciplinary action. Intentional circumvention, such as splitting purchases to avoid approval thresholds, is treated as a serious violation of the Code of Business Conduct.

10.2 Internal Audit tests compliance with this policy each year, including a sample of supplier file reviews, and reports results to the Audit Committee of the Board.

## 11. Related Policies

- Trade Secret Protection Policy (KPM-IP-001)
- Legal Review and Approval Policy (KPM-LG-001)
- Engineering Data Handling Policy (KPM-EN-003)
- Quality Management Policy (KPM-QA-001)
- Export Control Policy (KPM-CO-005)
- Anti-Bribery Policy (KPM-CO-002)
- Capital Expenditure Policy (KPM-FN-006)

## Appendix A. Scorecard Weights and Onboarding Checklist

A.1 **Scorecard weights.** The quarterly supplier scorecard combines the following weighted measures for production suppliers: quality (parts per million defective and corrective action closure), 35 percent; delivery (on-time and in-full), 30 percent; cost (price competitiveness and cost reduction contribution), 15 percent; responsiveness and communication, 10 percent; and sustainability and compliance, 10 percent. A score of 90 or above is rated preferred, 75 to 89 approved, 60 to 74 conditional and below 60 probation. Conditional suppliers receive an improvement plan, and suppliers on probation may not receive new business awards.

A.2 **Onboarding checklist.** The buyer ensures that the following are on file before the first order: completed supplier information form; tax documentation; bank verification record; qualification result; insurance certificates; quality manual acknowledgment; conflict minerals declaration where relevant; restricted-party screening result; information security questionnaire where relevant; and a signed acknowledgment of the supplier code of conduct.

A.3 **Supplier code of conduct.** Suppliers are asked to confirm in writing that they comply with the laws that apply to them; that they prohibit forced and child labor; that they provide a safe workplace; that they comply with environmental laws; that they do not offer or accept bribes; that they respect the intellectual property of others; and that they let Keystone verify compliance with reasonable notice.

A.4 **Dual sourcing.** For parts that account for more than 5 percent of a customer program's revenue, or that are made from long-lead material, the category manager considers a second source. Qualification of the second source starts with a sample order and a full first article inspection, and a trial lot must be accepted before the second source is added to the ASL for the part. The sourcing team records the split of volume between sources, which in normal conditions is no more than 80 percent to the primary source.

A.5 **Price changes and raw material surcharges.** Suppliers may request price increases only with documented justification, at least sixty days before the change, and with evidence such as index movements for raw material. The category manager reviews the request against the index and market, negotiates, and obtains the approval of the Vice President, Supply Chain for increases that exceed 3 percent on annual spend above $250,000. Surcharges for raw material are tied to published indices and reviewed quarterly.

## 12. Revision History

| Version | Date | Author | Summary of change |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.0 | August 8, 2018 | Director of Procurement | Initial release |
| 2.0 | May 20, 2021 | Vice President, Supply Chain | Added risk tiering and scorecard targets |
| 2.3 | February 6, 2024 | Vice President, Supply Chain | Added sub-tier and portal controls |
| 3.0 | January 15, 2025 | Vice President, Supply Chain | Revised section 3; aligned approval thresholds with Legal Review and Approval Policy |

# Quality Management Policy

**Keystone Precision Manufacturing, Inc.**
Policy owner: Director of Quality
Policy approver: Chief Operating Officer
Effective date: April 1, 2025
Review cycle: annually, and at each management review
Document number: KPM-QA-001

---

## 1. Purpose

1.1 Keystone Precision Manufacturing, Inc. ("Keystone") makes parts that fly, that are implanted, that carry fluids at high pressure and that hold heavy loads. A part that is out of tolerance may be an inconvenience in one application and a catastrophe in another. Customers choose Keystone because they trust that a part labeled with a given revision, material and tolerance really is that part, every time. This policy sets out how we earn and keep that trust.

1.2 The policy establishes Keystone's quality management system (QMS), which is certified to ISO 9001 at all plants, to AS9100 at the Dayton and Toledo plants, and to ISO 13485 at the Erie plant. It defines the quality principles that apply to every employee, assigns responsibility for the elements of the system and sets the minimum expectations for process control, inspection, nonconforming product, corrective action, calibration, supplier quality, training and continual improvement.

1.3 Quality is not the exclusive responsibility of the Quality department. Every operator, programmer, inspector, buyer, planner and manager contributes to it, and every person has the authority and the obligation to stop work when they believe a part is not right.

## 2. Scope and Definitions

2.1 **Scope.** This policy applies to all products and services that Keystone designs, makes, tests, packages or ships, at all plants and for all customers. It applies to all employees and to temporary workers. Elements of it flow down to Keystone's suppliers through the Supplier Engagement Policy.

2.2 **Definitions.**

- **Conformance:** fulfillment of a requirement of a drawing, specification, standard, customer instruction or regulation.
- **Nonconformance:** failure to fulfill a requirement.
- **First article inspection (FAI):** a complete, documented verification that a production process can make a part that meets all requirements, performed before the first production lot and after significant changes.
- **Key characteristic:** a feature of a part, identified by the customer or by Keystone, whose variation has a significant effect on fit, form, function, performance or safety.
- **Statistical process control (SPC):** the use of statistical methods to monitor and control a process.
- **Corrective action:** action to eliminate the cause of a nonconformance so that it does not recur.
- **Preventive action:** action to eliminate the cause of a potential nonconformance.
- **Material review board (MRB):** the cross-functional group that decides the disposition of nonconforming product.
- **Escape:** a nonconforming part that reaches a customer.

## 3. Quality Principles

3.1 **Customer focus.** We determine, understand and meet customer requirements, including the explicit requirements on drawings and purchase orders and the implicit requirement that the part will work as intended.

3.2 **Process approach.** We manage activities as interrelated processes with defined inputs, outputs, owners and measures. We understand variation and control it at its source rather than inspecting it out at the end.

3.3 **Prevention over detection.** Time spent in planning, fixturing, programming and proving out a process is cheaper than time spent in sorting and rework. We use failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA), control plans and error-proofing in new and changed processes.

3.4 **Evidence-based decisions.** We make decisions using data. Charts, capability studies and trend reports are posted in the cell where they are produced, so that the people who run the process can see how it is behaving.

3.5 **Stop-work authority.** Any employee may stop a process that is producing, or may produce, nonconforming product. No employee will be disciplined for exercising this authority in good faith. A supervisor who overrides a stop must notify the quality manager immediately.

3.6 **Continual improvement.** We set annual quality objectives, review performance at management reviews and invest in improvements through kaizen events, Six Sigma projects and employee suggestions.

## 4. Planning and Release of New Products

4.1 **Advanced product quality planning.** For new parts, the program manager leads a cross-functional team to plan the process using the APQP method. The plan covers design feasibility, process flow, FMEA, control plan, measurement system analysis, tooling and fixtures, gauges, packaging, and a schedule for FAI and production part approval.

4.2 **Feasibility review.** Before Keystone commits to a new part, engineering, manufacturing and quality review the drawing for manufacturability, tolerance stack-ups, material availability, special processes, inspection capability and any customer-specific quality requirements. Concerns are documented and resolved with the customer before quoting is completed.

4.3 **First article inspection.** FAI is performed in accordance with AS9102 or the customer's requirement. All characteristics, including notes, material and special process certifications, are verified and recorded. The FAI report is approved by Quality before shipment of production quantities. A full or partial FAI is repeated after a change in design, material, supplier, process, tooling, machine location or after a lapse in production exceeding twenty-four months.

4.4 **Production part approval.** Where customers require it, a production part approval package is submitted with dimensional results, capability studies, material and process certifications and sample parts. Shipments do not begin until the customer approves.

## 5. Process Control

5.1 **Work instructions and routers.** Each part has a router that lists the operations in order, the machine or workstation, the work instruction, the gauges and the inspection points. Only the released version may be used.

5.2 **Setup verification.** After setup and before each production run, the operator produces a first piece, which is inspected by the operator and verified by an inspector or lead before the run continues. The result is recorded in the traveler.

5.3 **In-process inspection.** Operators measure characteristics at the frequency defined in the control plan. For key characteristics, SPC is used. Control charts are reviewed each shift. Process capability (Cpk) must be at least 1.33 for key characteristics, or 1.67 where the customer requires it. If capability is not demonstrated, 100 percent inspection is applied until the process is improved.

5.4 **Special processes.** Special processes such as heat treatment, plating, anodizing, passivation, welding and non-destructive testing are performed only by processes and personnel qualified under the applicable specification. Pyrometry is performed in accordance with AMS2750, and records are kept for the life of the part plus the retention period required by the customer.

5.5 **Identification and traceability.** Material is identified by heat, lot or batch from receipt through shipment. Where customers require serialization, each part is individually marked and the traceability record links the part to the material, the machine, the operator, the inspection results and the shipment.

5.6 **Foreign object damage and debris.** Aerospace work areas follow foreign object damage prevention practices, including tool control, housekeeping, shadow boards and cleanliness checks at the end of each shift. Tools are counted at the start and end of shifts in areas designated by the quality manager.

5.7 **Handling, storage, packaging and preservation.** Parts are protected against damage, contamination and corrosion during handling, storage and shipment. Packaging specifications are defined for each part number. Shelf-life-limited materials are controlled through first-expired, first-out and are quarantined when they reach their limit.

## 6. Measurement and Calibration

6.1 **Calibration.** All gauges, instruments, test equipment and measuring machines that affect product quality are uniquely identified, calibrated at defined intervals against standards traceable to the National Institute of Standards and Technology, and labeled with the due date. Equipment that is overdue or found out of tolerance is removed from service immediately.

6.2 **Out-of-tolerance findings.** When an instrument is found out of tolerance at calibration, the calibration technician notifies the quality manager, who determines the effect on product measured since the previous calibration and decides whether a recall, re-inspection or customer notification is needed.

6.3 **Measurement system analysis.** Gauge repeatability and reproducibility studies are performed for key characteristics and whenever a gauge or method changes. The gauge's variation must consume no more than 10 percent of the tolerance for key characteristics; between 10 and 30 percent is acceptable only with the approval of the quality manager.

6.4 **Coordinate measuring machines.** Programs for coordinate measuring machines are controlled documents. Changes are verified against a master part before release. The CMM room is held at 68 degrees Fahrenheit, plus or minus one degree, and temperature records are reviewed weekly.

## 7. Nonconforming Product

7.1 **Identification and containment.** Nonconforming product is identified, tagged with a red label and segregated in a marked quarantine area. It must not be used, shipped or mixed with conforming product. Suspect product is held until it is evaluated.

7.2 **Material review board.** The MRB, composed of a representative of Quality, Engineering and Manufacturing, meets as needed to decide disposition: scrap, rework to the original requirement, repair, return to supplier or use as is. Use-as-is and repair dispositions require customer approval when the customer has reserved this right. All dispositions are recorded.

7.3 **Escapes.** If a nonconforming part is suspected to have been shipped, the quality manager must notify the customer within twenty-four hours of confirmation, begin containment at Keystone, the customer and any intermediaries, and open an investigation. The Director of Quality reports each escape to the Chief Operating Officer within one business day.

7.4 **Counterfeit and suspect parts.** Keystone buys only from authorized sources. Material found to be counterfeit, suspect or unapproved is quarantined, reported to the customer and, where required, to government authorities such as the Government-Industry Data Exchange Program.

## 8. Corrective and Preventive Action

8.1 A corrective action is opened for every customer complaint, internal escape, audit finding of major severity and repeated nonconformance. The owner responds with containment within twenty-four hours, a root cause analysis within ten business days, and a corrective action plan with owners and dates. Quality verifies effectiveness after ninety days.

8.2 Root cause analysis uses structured methods such as 5-Why, Ishikawa diagrams or 8D. "Operator error" is not accepted as a root cause without explanation of why the system allowed the error.

8.3 Lessons from corrective actions are shared across plants through the monthly quality review, and process FMEAs are updated.

## 9. Audits and Management Review

9.1 **Internal audits.** The Quality department maintains an annual audit schedule that covers every process and every shift at each plant. Auditors are trained and independent of the area audited. Findings are classified as major, minor or opportunity, and are tracked until closed.

9.2 **External audits.** Registrar and customer audits are coordinated by the quality manager of the plant. The Director of Quality is notified of any major finding within one business day.

9.3 **Management review.** The Chief Operating Officer chairs the management review each quarter. Inputs include customer feedback, on-time delivery, parts per million defective, cost of poor quality, audit results, corrective action status, supplier performance and risks. Outputs are decisions on improvement, resources and objectives.

## 10. Training and Competence

10.1 Each job has a competency matrix that lists the required skills, training and certifications. Operators are certified on a machine or process by a qualified trainer before working unsupervised. Inspectors are certified annually in visual standards and measuring methods.

10.2 Quality awareness training is part of new hire orientation and is repeated annually. Topics include the quality policy, stop-work authority, the importance of traceability, foreign object prevention and the consequences of nonconformance.

## 11. Roles and Responsibilities

11.1 **Chief Operating Officer.** Sponsors the QMS, chairs management reviews and ensures resources are available.

11.2 **Director of Quality.** Owns this policy, maintains certifications, represents Keystone to registrars and customers on quality matters and approves quality procedures.

11.3 **Plant quality managers.** Implement the QMS at the plant, manage inspection and metrology, chair the MRB and lead corrective actions.

11.4 **Plant managers.** Ensure that production processes follow the control plan and that quality is not compromised for schedule.

11.5 **Supervisors and leads.** Verify setups, monitor in-process checks, and ensure operators have the training and equipment they need.

11.6 **Operators and inspectors.** Follow work instructions, record results accurately, identify nonconforming product and exercise stop-work authority.

11.7 **Supplier quality engineers.** Qualify and monitor suppliers and manage supplier corrective actions.

## 12. Exceptions

12.1 Requests to deviate from a procedure in this policy are submitted to the Director of Quality, who may approve a temporary deviation for up to ninety days if product quality and customer requirements are not compromised. Longer deviations require the approval of the Chief Operating Officer.

12.2 Customer-imposed requirements that differ from this policy are recorded in the project plan and followed unless they conflict with law.

## 13. Enforcement

13.1 Falsification of inspection records, shipment of known nonconforming product without disposition, or disregard of stop-work authority are serious violations that may result in termination and, where required, in notification of customers and regulators.

13.2 Employees may report quality concerns, including pressure to ship nonconforming product, to the Director of Quality, to Human Resources or through the ethics line, without fear of retaliation.

## 14. Related Policies

- Supplier Engagement Policy (KPM-SC-004)
- Engineering Data Handling Policy (KPM-EN-003)
- Environmental Health and Safety Policy (KPM-EH-001)
- Code of Business Conduct (KPM-CO-001)

## Appendix A. Quality Metrics, Audit Checklist and Worked Examples

A.1 **Core metrics.** The following metrics are reported monthly for each plant and consolidated for the quarterly management review.

| Metric | Definition | Corporate target |
|---|---|---|
| On-time delivery | Lines shipped on or before the promised date divided by lines due | 96 percent or better |
| Customer parts per million (PPM) | Nonconforming parts returned by customers per million shipped | Below 150 |
| Internal first-pass yield | Parts accepted at final inspection without rework | 97 percent or better |
| Scrap and rework cost | Cost of scrapped and reworked product as a share of sales | Below 1.8 percent |
| Corrective action timeliness | Corrective actions closed by their due date | 90 percent or better |
| Calibration on-time rate | Instruments calibrated by their due date | 100 percent |
| Supplier PPM | Nonconforming parts received per million, by supplier | Below 500 |
| Escapes | Number of confirmed nonconforming parts shipped to a customer | Zero |

A.2 **Reading a control chart.** Operators and leads should know the basic signals that a process has changed. A single point beyond a control limit calls for an immediate check of the part and the process. Seven consecutive points on one side of the center line, or seven points steadily rising or falling, indicate a shift or trend even if every point is inside the limits. A run of points hugging the center line may mean the sample is hiding variation, for instance because measurements from two machines are being mixed. When a signal appears, the operator stops, contains the parts made since the last good check, notes the time and calls the lead. Adjustments are made only when a signal shows that the process has changed; adjusting a stable process increases variation.

A.3 **Process audit checklist.** Internal auditors use the following questions in each area. Is the current released revision of the router and drawing available at the point of use? Does the operator know the key characteristics and the reaction plan? Are gauges identified, within calibration and appropriate for the tolerance? Are first-piece records complete for the last three setups? Are nonconforming parts tagged and in quarantine? Is material identification maintained? Are tools and fixtures stored properly and checked for wear? Is housekeeping at the level required to prevent foreign object damage? Has training been recorded for everyone working in the area? Are customer-specific instructions posted?

A.4 **Worked example: a drifting bore.** A night-shift operator on a horizontal machining center measures a bore diameter on every fifth part and plots the result. Over six parts the readings move steadily toward the upper limit, though each remains within tolerance. The operator recognizes the trend, stops after the sixth part, and measures the last five parts made since the previous check. All five conform. The lead checks tool wear and finds the finishing boring bar is worn on its insert. The insert is changed, the first piece is checked and verified by the inspector, and the run continues. The operator records the event, the parts affected and the action taken on the traveler. Because the trend was caught before any part left the tolerance band, no nonconforming product was made, and no corrective action was needed; the tool life setting for that operation is updated by the process engineer the following morning so that the insert is changed earlier.

A.5 **Worked example: customer complaint.** A customer reports that three of fifty parts in a recent lot have a burr on an internal cross-hole that interferes with assembly. The customer service representative logs the complaint and notifies the plant quality manager, who opens a corrective action the same day. Containment includes inspecting stock at Keystone and in transit and sending a sorting team to the customer, if requested. Within ten business days, the team shows that a deburring step was moved to another operation during a routing change and the new instruction did not specify the cross-hole. The root cause is the routing change process, which did not require review of operations with deburring notes. Corrective action adds that review to the engineering change checklist and a verification step to the first-piece inspection. After ninety days, Quality confirms that no recurrence has occurred in three lots, and closes the corrective action.

A.6 **Cost of poor quality.** Finance and Quality jointly report the cost of poor quality each quarter, grouped as prevention (training, planning, calibration), appraisal (inspection, testing, audits), internal failure (scrap, rework, downtime) and external failure (returns, warranty, sorting, expediting). The report is used to prioritize improvement projects and to show whether investments in prevention are reducing failure costs.
